the inner ear uses three unconventional myosin isoforms to perform specialized functions.

the role of unconventional myosins in inner-ear sensory epithelia.
the identification and characterization of the unconventional myosins in the inner ear.
the identification of the myosin isomers that are present in the inner ear and with the localization and distribution of these myosin isomer within the hair cells of the inner ear.

these three unconventional myosin isoforms have specific and unique functions in inner ear sensory epithelia.

the unconventional myosins of the inner ear are not randomly distributed, but instead, are localized to specific subcellular compartments, where they presumably participate in specific cellular functions.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the myosin-I, -V, and -VI are involved in hair bundle formation and maintenance, and the myosin-VIII is required for the stereocilia tip link formation.

the inner-ear sensory epithelium is a rich source of myosin diversity, with each isozyme being differentially localized to actin-rich structures, and that these isozymes may be involved in diverse cellular functions.
unconventional myosins play important roles in the development and functioning of the hair bundle.
The main takeaway from our work is that
myosin is a very important motor for the actin filaments in the stereocilia of inner-ear hair cells.
the inner ear is an ideal tissue to study myosins because it has so many actin-rich domains that are differentially populated by myosins.
myosin is not a single molecule, but a large family of isozymes that are differentially expressed in cells, and that these isozymes are likely to have specific functions.
